body:
This issue indexes an idea hunt for gitcraft. It ran in three waves of research agents: Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1-sol at high reasoning, six in the first wave and four in each of the others. They looked at other git clients' feature pages and changelogs, the most-upvoted requests in their issue trackers, newer tools (jj, Sapling, GitButler, Graphite, git-branchless), adjacent software, and Git 2.40–2.56. Every wave was given everything already filed and asked only for new ideas. Each idea was checked against the README, the manual and `src/` on `dev`. After merging duplicates that's about 190 ideas, in 19 themed issues. They're only suggestions: take whatever fits and close the rest.

The third wave still turned up new ideas (7 to 14 per agent), but they were getting more specialised, so the hunt stopped there.

## Where I'd start

These come from across the issues. Each is small to medium, useful every day, and mostly reuses code gitcraft already has.

1. **Single instance** (#47). This is a bug as much as an idea: a second `gitcraft` process writes the same storage, and whichever window closes last wins, so the other window's tabs are lost.
2. **Force push with lease when a push is refused** (#32). Quick edits, rebase, amend and undo all rewrite history, and the push that follows them then fails, with no way out in the app.
3. **A conflict warning before merge, rebase or cherry-pick** (#32), from `git merge-tree --write-tree`.
4. **Fold staged changes into an older commit** (#33), with fixup and autosquash.
5. **Drag and drop in the graph** (#38).
6. **A reflog browser and lost-commit recovery** (#32).
7. **What changed between two versions of a branch or pull request** (#33, #35), using `range-diff`.
8. **Ranked palette results and shortcuts for the main actions** (#38).
9. **Keyboard focus and contrast** (#39).
10. **Bisect** (#34). Running it in parallel on a remote machine would be something no other client can do.

## Wave 1: broad survey

- #32 Safety nets for scary operations (15)
- #33 Reshaping history and stacked branches (15)
- #34 Tests, bisect and the remote machines (9)
- #35 Reviewing pull requests (11)
- #36 Understanding a repository's history (8)
- #37 Everyday git features other clients have (13)
- #38 UI / UX polish (14)
- #39 Accessibility (5)

## Wave 2: personas, the long tail, integrations, visualisation

- #40 Diffs for every kind of file (17)
- #41 Binary-heavy repositories (3)
- #42 Maintainers, releases and review without pull requests (8)
- #43 Integrations (8)
- #44 Small gaps other clients' users keep asking for (9)
- #45 Learning git, touring a repository, moving to a new machine (3)
- #46 Visualising history, and a little delight (8)

## Wave 3: the OS, coding agents, new git, borrowed patterns

- #47 The app shell and the OS (15)
- #48 Working with coding agents (11)
- #49 Remotes, submodules, configuration and git internals (14)
- #50 Staging, conflicts and history, borrowed from other kinds of apps (5)
title: Feature ideas: index of the idea hunt (19 issues, about 190 ideas)

body:
These ideas take patterns from software that has nothing to do with git (Photoshop, Dropbox, Obsidian, spreadsheets, Google Docs) and apply them to staging, conflicts and history. They come from the third and last round of the idea hunt. Take whatever fits and close the rest.

- [ ] **Three-state staging lens (M).** Open a partly staged file as three aligned versions: **HEAD → staged → working copy**. Click either boundary to stage or unstage lines. It marks the case where a later working edit undoes a staged one, so the file looks unchanged while the next commit still changes it.
  _Inspired by:_ layers in Photoshop, where each step stays visible on its own.

- [ ] **The original inside a conflict (M).** Each conflict card in the conflict editor gets an **Original** section. Expanding it shows what each side inserted and deleted relative to the base, so "one side deleted the validation, the other changed it" is visible before you choose. The parser already keeps diff3's base text, but the cards leave it out. The base can also come from the index. When there is no base, the card says so.
  _Inspired by:_ suggestion mode in Google Docs, which keeps the original text in view.

- [ ] **Keep both versions of a binary conflict (M).** For an asset that can't be merged, _Keep both…_ previews the two file names it would write, and shows each version's origin and size. Both are kept as ordinary files, and you check the result before it's staged. It warns that references to a renamed asset may need updating. Choosing ours or theirs would throw away someone's artwork; this doesn't.
  _Inspired by:_ [Dropbox's conflicted copies](https://help.dropbox.com/organize/conflicted-copy).

- [ ] **Commit backlinks (M).** A commit's details list the later commits that mention its hash: reverts, `Fixes:` trailers and plain mentions in messages. Each entry shows the matching text, and explicit links are kept apart from bare mentions. A click opens that commit's diff. This answers "what happened after this commit?" without knowing what to search for.
  _Inspired by:_ [Obsidian's backlinks](https://obsidian.md/help/plugins/backlinks).

- [ ] **File versions across branches (M).** Pick several release branches and a folder. Files are the rows and branches the columns. Cells with identical content share a marker, and missing files and mode changes are shown as such. Select two cells to open their diff. This answers "which releases still have a different version of this config?" without comparing branches pair by pair.
  _Inspired by:_ comparing columns in a spreadsheet.
title: Ideas: staging, conflicts and history, borrowed from other kinds of apps

body:
These are ideas about remotes, submodules, subtrees, configuration and git's internals: things a GUI rarely shows, plus what Git 2.40–2.56 make possible. They come from the third round of the idea hunt. They're only suggestions, so take whatever fits and close the rest.

"Established" means the feature is older than Git 2.40; newer requirements are named. Effort is rough: **S** is a contained addition, **M** is a new view or a coordinated flow, **L** means new state and integration work.

## Most useful

- [ ] **Pull from one remote, push to another (M).** Each branch shows two routes, for example _Pull from origin/main_ and _Push to fork/dev_. Each route has its own ahead / behind counts and a picker to change it. gitcraft's own checkout works like this (`origin` is upstream, `fork` is the user's fork), but the upstream dialog only knows one destination for both directions.
  _Git:_ established `branch.<name>.pushRemote` and `remote.pushDefault` ([docs](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config#Documentation/git-config.txt-branchnamepushRemote)).

- [ ] **Which configuration wins, and from which file (M).** Pick a setting, such as the pull strategy, signing or line endings. gitcraft shows:
  - the value in effect, with its file and scope;
  - the values it overrides, underneath;
  - where gitcraft's profile config and `includeIf` sections fit in.

  _Remove this override_ lets the repository inherit again, and the result can be compared between worktrees. Only allowlisted settings are shown, and anything credential-related is hidden. This answers "why does git behave differently here?"
  _Inspired by:_ the computed styles in [Chrome DevTools](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/css/reference). _Git:_ established `config --show-origin --show-scope --includes`; 2.56 adds `includeIf` conditions on the worktree's location.

- [ ] **Tracked files missing from Changes (S).** A small diagnostics view lists the paths marked `assume-unchanged` or `skip-worktree` (`ls-files -v`). It explains the difference between the two, offers to clear flags set by mistake, and keeps entries managed by sparse-checkout apart from manual flags.
  _Git:_ established ([update-index](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-update-index)).

- [ ] **Publish submodule changes before their parent (M).** Before the superproject is pushed, list the submodule commits it points to that haven't been published yet. _Push dependencies, then parent_ pushes them in that order and reports each repository's result. It also says which remote was checked, since "on some remote" doesn't mean every collaborator can reach it.
  _Git:_ established `push --recurse-submodules=check|on-demand`.

- [ ] **Submodule conflicts as graphs (M).** A conflicted submodule pointer opens the submodule's graph around base, ours and theirs. Pick an existing commit that contains both sides, or open the submodule to merge there. Either way, the chosen commit is recorded in the parent.

## Remotes

- [ ] **Remote refspec editor (M).** Choose which branches or ref prefixes a remote fetches, and exclude some (negative refspecs). Set different fetch and push URLs, and see how mirroring behaves. A preview shows each mapping, for example `refs/heads/release/* → refs/remotes/vendor/release/*`, and what pruning would delete. Today a remote has a single URL in gitcraft.

- [ ] **Publish to several hosts (M).** A publication group, for example GitHub, GitLab and a backup server, is pushed in one go. Each destination reports its own result, and a retry only goes to the ones that failed. It says plainly that the pushes aren't atomic.
  _Git:_ 2.55 adds pushing to remote groups ([release notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/git/git/master/Documentation/RelNotes/2.55.0.adoc)).

- [ ] **Push outbox (L).** _Queue push_ while offline records the exact commit, the remote and the branch. Commits made later don't silently join it. When the network is back, send the entries you choose, or let plain pushes go out on their own. If the history was rewritten, the destination changed or the push is rejected, the entry pauses for review.
  _Inspired by:_ email clients' offline outbox.

## Subtrees and topology

- [ ] **Subtrees (L).** Register a vendored folder's source repository and branch. From there, pull its upstream changes, look at the local edits, or split them out and send them back. It explains the difference between a squashed import and one with full history.
  _Git:_ `git subtree` (in contrib, often installed); 2.51 adds signing.

- [ ] **Shared and borrowed objects (M).** Show which repositories share one git directory and which borrow objects through alternates. It points out donor paths that have gone missing, and _Make this clone independent_ copies the objects it needs before the link is removed.
  _Git:_ established alternates; `git repo info` (2.52, more keys in 2.56).

## Internals

- [ ] **All refs (M).** Browse the refs outside branches and tags: root refs, bisect refs, `refs/original/*` backups, application refs and `refs/namespaces/*`. Follow symbolic refs, look at the object each ref points to, and show the history of a namespace.
  _Git:_ 2.45 `for-each-ref --include-root-refs`, 2.51 `--start-after`.

- [ ] **Replace refs and grafts (M).** Mark the commits that replace refs affect, and switch between the original history and the effective one (`--no-replace-objects`). Two imported histories can be joined temporarily with a graft, and the link stays visible and removable.

- [ ] **How an object is stored (M).** Paste an object ID, or pick a file version. gitcraft shows its type, size, packed size, packfile and delta chain, and you can follow tree entries and delta bases from there. This explains one object rather than the totals that the health page in #37 would show.
  _Git:_ `cat-file --batch-check`, `verify-pack -v`.

- [ ] **Reftable: see it and migrate to it (M).** Show whether a repository stores refs as files or as reftable, and what that means for other installed tools. A guided migration runs `git refs migrate` and checks the result afterwards. It refuses linked worktrees, and other programs writing to the repository have to be stopped first.
  _Git:_ 2.45 adds the reftable backend, 2.46 adds `refs migrate`.

Also, about the _dubious ownership_ card in #47: local discovery can reduce that error to "not inside a git repository" today. The card only helps if the real reason is kept.
title: Ideas: remotes, submodules, configuration and git internals

body:
These are ideas for working with coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Aider: seeing what they wrote, reviewing it one step at a time, steering them, and fencing them in. They come from the third round of the idea hunt. Agent worktrees, AI commit messages, reviewer echo and AI objections with reproducers are already in #34, #35 and #37, so they aren't repeated here. These are only suggestions: take whatever fits and close the rest.

Effort is rough. **S** is a contained addition, **M** is a new view or a coordinated flow, and **L** is new state and integration work.

## Most useful

- [ ] **Agent turns as review steps (M).** Optional agent hooks (Claude Code's Stop / PostToolUse, Codex's notify) call `gitcraft checkpoint`. That saves the tree after each agent turn under `refs/gitcraft/agent/<session>/<n>`. _Uncommitted changes_ then shows a strip of turns, each labelled with its prompt.
  - Review turn 4 on its own, or everything since you last looked. Hunks you marked as reviewed stay hidden while they don't change.
  - _Revert this turn only_ takes back that turn's diff and keeps the later ones.

  _Closest:_ Cursor's checkpoints and Claude Code's `/rewind`. Both live inside one agent's own UI and are gone after the session.

- [ ] **Hand it to the agent (S–M).** Write local line comments on any diff, without publishing them. They collect in a tray. _Send to agent_ types them into that worktree's agent terminal as one message, or hands them over through the MCP server below, and then clears them. The same button works elsewhere too:
  - on a conflict, it sends the three sides;
  - on a failing CI run, the log excerpt;
  - on a pull-request thread, the thread with its file and line.

  It can reuse the pending-comment model of the pull-request review.
  _Seen in:_ [Conductor's diff comments](https://conductor.build/docs/guides/review-and-merge), which work only for its own agents, not across forges or for conflicts.

- [ ] **AI authorship lens (M).** gitcraft reads the line attribution that agents record about themselves. That is git-ai's `refs/notes/ai`, Agent Trace records, and agent co-author trailers. From it, gitcraft shows:
  - a human / agent / mixed stripe in blame and in diff gutters;
  - a robot badge on graph rows, and a filter for agent-written commits;
  - per-branch figures such as _71% agent-written, 9% of that since edited by a person_.

  It never guesses from the code itself.
  _Seen in:_ [git-ai](https://github.com/git-ai-project/git-ai) (a CLI) and the [Agent Trace spec](https://github.com/cursor/agent-trace). No git GUI shows it.

- [ ] **Worktree setup recipe (S–M).** A recipe per repository runs whenever a worktree is made, for an agent or not. It does three things:
  - copies or links ignored files from the main worktree (`.env.local`, `node_modules`, build caches);
  - runs a setup command;
  - sets environment variables per worktree, such as `PORT=3000+n` or a separate `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`.

  It runs on the repository's machine, WSL and SSH included. This answers the most common complaint about one worktree per agent: a fresh worktree is missing everything that's ignored, and its servers fight the others for ports.
  _Seen in:_ Conductor's setup scripts, worktree CLIs.

## Bigger

- [ ] **Bake-off between attempts (M–L).** Select 2–4 worktrees or branches that tried the same task from the same base. A grid compares the files each one touched, its size, the new dependencies it brings in and whether it builds. Any file can be opened side by side across them. _Assemble_ builds a new branch from file X of attempt A and a hunk of attempt B.
  _Closest:_ [Superset's "race agents"](https://docs.superset.sh/recipes/race-agents) and [Emdash best-of-N](https://docs.emdash.sh/best-of-n). Neither assembles a winner hunk by hunk.

- [ ] **gitcraft as an MCP server (M–L).** `gitcraft mcp` lets agents read the graph, status, blame, attribution, conflicts and CI results. Agents can run only the operations gitcraft can undo. Each one goes into the undo list with a robot badge, so Ctrl+Z also works on what the agent did. Destructive requests (force push, deleting a branch, hard reset) wait in the window as an _Approve / Deny_ card, with the ghost-run preview where one exists.
  _Closest:_ [GitKraken's MCP server](https://www.gitkraken.com/features/mcp-server), which asks for confirmations but has no undo shared with the user.

- [ ] **The prompt behind a commit (M–L).** A commit's details get a _Prompt & session_ tab. It shows the prompts, the agent's summary and the tool calls that touched each hunk. Clicking a hunk jumps to the step that wrote it. The sources are:
  - Entire's checkpoints branch;
  - the prompts GitButler writes into commit messages;
  - local Claude Code and Codex transcripts, matched by worktree and time.

  Transcripts are only shown locally. The push dialog warns when a checkpoints branch would be pushed.
  _Seen in:_ [Entire](https://docs.entire.io/cli/overview) (a CLI with a web view), GitButler.

- [ ] **Flags for weakened checks (S–M).** A file or hunk gets a _weakens checks_ badge when it:
  - removes assertions or deletes test files;
  - adds `#[ignore]`, `skip` or `assert True`, or loosens tolerances;
  - rewrites snapshot files wholesale;
  - changes CI with `continue-on-error`, a removed job or `--no-verify`.

  It works only from the diff, the same way every time, and shows its evidence.
  _Like:_ [tampercheck](https://pypi.org/project/tampercheck/) and [hallucinot](https://github.com/jayj221/hallucinot), which are CLIs.

- [ ] **Agent fence (M).** One list per repository of paths that agents must stay out of: secrets, `.github/workflows`, migrations, lockfiles. gitcraft writes the list into each agent's own config (Claude's deny rules, `.cursorignore`, Codex). Any agent worktree whose changes or untracked files touch a fenced path turns red, and merging it back needs an explicit confirmation. Deny rules [can leak](https://dev.to/umangcirvix/protecting-env-secrets-from-ai-agents-six-layers-and-how-to-test-each-one-2g8l), for example through scripts the agent runs, so gitcraft checks the result rather than trusting the rule.

- [ ] **Scope drift meter (M).** It compares the task (the agent worktree's prompt, or its linked issue) with what changed, for example: _asked to fix login; also touched 14 files in 5 unrelated folders, added 2 dependencies, changed 3 public signatures, 40% formatting only_. Each item opens its files. The figures that can be measured exactly come first, and matching them against the task with an LLM is optional.

- [ ] **Collision matrix for parallel agent branches (M).** This builds on the conflict warning in #32. For N agent branches, it shows an N×N `merge-tree` matrix and suggests the order to land them in with the fewest conflicts.
title: Ideas: working with coding agents (turn-by-turn review, attribution, MCP, fences)

body:
These are ideas for the app around the repository view: how gitcraft fits into the OS, how it survives crashes and bad networks, and how it reports problems. They come from the third round of the idea hunt, after checking `src/main.rs`, `src/app/`, `src/update/`, `src/remote/askpass.rs`, `src/forge/http.rs` and the installer. They're only suggestions, so take whatever fits and close the rest.

Effort is rough: **S** a contained addition, **M** a new view or a coordinated flow, **L** a larger rework.

## Most useful

- [ ] **A second launch goes to the window that's already open (S–M).** Running `gitcraft path` or _Open in gitcraft_ while gitcraft is running opens a tab in the running window, or focuses it. Today `main.rs` always starts a new process. Two processes then write the same eframe storage (open tabs, recents, settings), and whichever closes last wins, so the other window's tabs are lost. The handoff can work like `remote/askpass.rs` does: a 127.0.0.1 listener with a token.
  _Seen in:_ VS Code, GitHub Desktop.

- [ ] **Commands for the terminal and for files in Explorer, Finder and Nautilus (M).**
  - `gitcraft .` from a subfolder opens the repository it's in.
  - `gitcraft log <file>`, `gitcraft blame <file>:<line>`, `gitcraft show <rev>` and `gitcraft compare a..b` open those views directly.
  - The installer adds _History in gitcraft_ and _Blame in gitcraft_ to files' menus (Windows `*\shell` verbs, `.desktop` Actions, macOS Services). Today only folders get an entry.

  This needs the single-instance handoff above. TortoiseGit-style overlay icons are deliberately left out: Windows has only about 15 overlay slots, and status caches freeze Explorer.
  _Seen in:_ [Tower's `gittower`](https://www.git-tower.com/help/guides/integration/cli-tool/mac).

- [ ] **Links from the browser into gitcraft (M).** Register a `gitcraft://` scheme: the registry on Windows, `x-scheme-handler` on Linux, `CFBundleURLTypes` on macOS. `gitcraft://open?url=https://codeberg.org/o/r/pulls/12` finds the local clone by its remote URL among the recents and open tabs, then opens that pull request, commit or `file#L40`. If there's no clone, it offers to clone. Pasting any forge URL into the palette or the start page does the same. This is the other direction from _Copy link / Open on forge_ in #43.
  _Seen in:_ GitHub Desktop (`x-github-client://openRepo`), [GitKraken deep links](https://help.gitkraken.com/gitkraken-desktop/linking/), `gittower://`.

- [ ] **Explain a git error, with a button that fixes it (M).** Match git's error text against known failures and show a card with the fix:
  - _dubious ownership_ → **Trust this folder** adds `safe.directory` for that path only, never `*`;
  - _index.lock exists_ → shows how old the lock is and whether git is running, then **Remove stale lock**;
  - CRLF warnings → what `core.autocrlf` would do and what `.gitattributes` would do;
  - _Filename too long_ → `core.longpaths`;
  - _SSL certificate problem_ → `http.sslBackend=schannel`;
  - _RPC failed / early EOF / HTTP 413_, _unrelated histories_, _shallow update not allowed_;
  - _Permission denied (publickey)_ → the SSH helper in #43.

  It would live in a new `git/errors.rs`.

- [ ] **What you typed survives a crash or a restart (S–M).** Nothing typed is saved today: not the commit message, not unsent pull-request comments and replies, not an interactive-rebase list being edited. Save them per repository every few seconds. A marker written at start and cleared on a normal close leads to _gitcraft closed unexpectedly: your drafts and tabs were restored_.
  _Seen in:_ VS Code hot exit.

## Smaller

- [ ] **Diagnostics for bug reports (S–M).** _Help → Copy diagnostics_ collects:
  - the version and channel, the OS, and the wgpu adapter and backend;
  - the versions of git, `gh`, `glab` and `tea`, and whether each is signed in (never tokens);
  - an allowlist of `git config --show-origin` keys;
  - the last panic, from a panic hook that writes a log in the data folder;
  - the recent operations, with paths redacted.

  It then opens a prefilled issue.

- [ ] **Connection doctor and proxy page (M).** Settings → Network shows the proxy each part uses:
  - git (`http.proxy` and the environment);
  - the forge client;
  - ssh (`ProxyCommand` / `ProxyJump`).

  _Test connection_ on a remote checks DNS, TCP, the TLS chain (with custom CAs), authentication and how long `ls-remote` takes. It names the step that failed, for example "407: the proxy wants a password".

- [ ] **Offline and metered mode (S–M).** A switch, or detection (Windows reports metered networks), pauses background fetch, avatars, update downloads and the CI and pull-request polling. The toolbar says _offline: last fetched 3 h ago_, and network buttons say why they're off instead of hanging.

- [ ] **Taskbar progress, jump list and dock menu (M).** The taskbar button shows progress during a clone, fetch or push, and turns red if it fails. A jump list (Windows), dock menu (macOS) or `.desktop` Actions (Linux) lists the recent repositories plus _Clone…_ and _Open…_. With `unsafe_code = "forbid"`, the COM calls need a wrapper crate.

- [ ] **A tray icon that keeps watching (M–L, opt-in).** _Keep running in the tray when closed_: recent repositories keep being fetched. The tray says "main moved 6 commits", "review requested" or "checks failed on your branch", and its menu lists the repositories. GNOME has no tray, so there it falls back to notifications.

- [ ] **Portable mode (S).** A `gitcraft.portable` file or a `data/` folder next to the executable keeps settings, profiles, the avatar cache and the profiles' `.gitconfig` files there instead of `%APPDATA%`. The updater replaces the files in that folder, and the credential store becomes optional. This is for USB sticks and locked-down machines.
  _Seen in:_ SourceGit, Git Extensions.

- [ ] **HTTPS sign-ins page (S–M).** It shows which credential helper is in effect for each host, and which account it holds. _Sign out of github.com_ runs `git credential reject`. A 401 or 403 right after signing in is recognised as "the wrong account is stored", with a button to switch accounts. That is the classic Git Credential Manager trap. This page is the HTTPS counterpart of _Forget saved SSH sign-ins_.

- [ ] **Lazy tabs, and suspending idle ones (M).** Restored tabs load only when first shown, so 15 saved tabs no longer mean 15 history loads and 15 folder watchers at startup. Tabs left alone for a while drop their graph and diff caches and stop watching until they're focused again.
  _Seen in:_ browsers' tab discarding.

- [ ] **Undo an update, or stay on a version (S).** The updater keeps the previous binary. _Go back to 0.3.3_ swaps it back and pins that version until you unpin it. Today only "skip this release" exists.

- [ ] **Localization (L).** Every string is hard-coded in English, including the tables in `manual.rs`. Moving them to Fluent would let gitcraft be translated, as SourceGit is. egui's right-to-left support is weak, so right-to-left languages would come later.
title: Ideas: the app shell and the OS (single instance, deep links, error fixes, crash recovery)

body:
These are ideas for seeing a repository's history in new ways, and for a little delight. They're from the second round of the idea hunt. They're only suggestions, so take whatever fits and close the rest.

Most of them can use egui's `Painter`, clipping and textures. gitcraft already turns on wgpu, so a custom paint callback is available where shaders help. The analysis behind them should run off the UI thread and say how much history it covered.

## Graph

- [ ] **Lanes by branching model (M).** `main`, release branches and feature branches each keep a horizontal band and a stable colour across reloads. You pick a simple model, or pin a branch to a band.
  _Seen in:_ [git-graph](https://github.com/git-bahn/git-graph).

- [ ] **History minimap (M).** A small map of the loaded history's shape, with a rectangle for the part in view, plus HEAD, tags and search hits. Dragging the rectangle moves through history. The point where older history isn't loaded yet is marked.

## Whole-repository views

- [ ] **Activity calendar (M).** Browse activity by day or by month. Click a day to see its commits, or drag across dates to select a period. You choose author date or committer date, and each commit is counted once across refs.
  _Like:_ [git-quick-stats](https://github.com/git-quick-stats/git-quick-stats) (heatmaps, not clickable).

- [ ] **Churn and contributor atlas (L).** A zoomable treemap of the folders. Files are sized by bytes or by how often they change, and coloured by recent churn or by their most frequent contributor. You can change the time window, and clicking a hotspot opens its file history. Labels say "most frequent contributor", not "owner".
  _Seen in:_ [Git Truck](https://git-truck.github.io/git-truck/docs/).

- [ ] **Watch the repository grow (L).** Play or scrub through an animation of the file tree. Files appear, change and disappear, and contributors light up where they work. Pause on any moment to open its commit.
  _Seen in:_ [Gource](https://gource.io/).

- [ ] **Contributor statistics (S–M).** Commits, files touched and active periods for each author over a chosen time. It follows `.mailmap` so one person counts once.
  _Seen in:_ SourceGit 2026.22.

## Delight

- [ ] **Quiet celebrations (M, opt-in).** A short flourish for the first commit of a repository, a release tag, or a merge that finished, with an optional soft sound. It plays only after the operation has succeeded. Sound and motion each have their own switch, and it never rewards commit counts or numbers of changed lines.
  _Like:_ [Commit Confetti](https://github.com/is-harshul/commit-confetti).

- [ ] **History postcards (M).** Export a composed PNG of a release's graph: the commit range, the release name, the date and, if you want, the contributors' names. A preview shows which names and messages will appear, with an option to anonymise them. It's for release announcements and anniversaries.
  _Like:_ [Git-sonar](https://github.com/JonathanRReed/Git-sonar).
title: Ideas: visualising history, and a little delight

body:
These ideas are for learning git, getting into a new repository, and taking your setup to a new machine. They came from the second round of the idea hunt. Take whatever fits and close the rest.

- [ ] **Practice repositories and a glossary (M).**
  - The start page gets a _Practice_ entry. It makes a throwaway repository with a ready-made scenario: a merge conflict, a diverged branch, a detached HEAD, or "undo a commit that was already pushed".
  - Each scenario has a goal and a check that says when it's solved.
  - Hovering words such as HEAD, upstream, fast-forward and rebase anywhere in the UI explains them.
  - `repo/samples.rs` already makes demo repositories.

  _Closest:_ Learn Git Branching and Oh My Git!, which are a web page and a game rather than a real client.

- [ ] **A tour of this repository (M).** A generated first-day page. It shows:
  - an excerpt of the README;
  - the workflow worked out from history: squash or merge commits, Conventional Commits, signed commits, DCO;
  - the branch and tag scheme (`release/*`, `v*`);
  - who has been active in each top folder over the last 90 days, and the files that change most;
  - what the repository needs: LFS, submodules, husky or lefthook, `.editorconfig`;
  - the contributing rules and the pull request template.

  A setup checklist follows, where each item is a button: _Install LFS hooks_, _Set an identity for this host_, and so on.
  _Closest:_ [onefetch](https://github.com/o2sh/onefetch), in the terminal.

- [ ] **New machine, same setup (S–M).** _Export setup_ writes one file. It holds the profiles, the settings, the saved identities and each recent repository's remotes, its own author and its hidden branches. _Import_ on the new machine lists the repositories. The ones you pick are cloned, with their worktrees and their per-repository config restored.
  _Closest:_ GitKraken's account sync, which goes through their cloud.
title: Ideas: learning git, touring a repository, moving to a new machine

body:
These are small gaps that users of other clients keep asking for. Most come from the most-upvoted open feature requests in GitHub Desktop's, Sublime Merge's, Fork's and lazygit's trackers, which I read with `gh` on 2026-11-06 (👍 counts at that time). None of them is in gitcraft yet. They're only suggestions, so take whatever fits and close the rest.

- [ ] **gitcraft as `git difftool` / `mergetool`, and comparing any two files (M).** `gitcraft --diff A B` and `gitcraft --merge BASE LOCAL REMOTE MERGED` would open gitcraft's own diff and its three-pane conflict editor on files outside a repository. Settings would register gitcraft in git's config. This is the reverse of "external diff and merge tools" in #37.
  _Asked for:_ [sublime_merge#40](https://github.com/sublimehq/sublime_merge/issues/40) (77 👍), [lazygit#1492](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit/issues/1492) (23), [sublime_merge#434](https://github.com/sublimehq/sublime_merge/issues/434).

- [ ] **Pin branches, and sort them by last commit (S).** Pinned branches stay at the top of _Local_. A switch sorts the rest by name or by most recent commit (`for-each-ref --sort=-committerdate`). Both are kept per repository.
  _Asked for:_ [desktop#15767](https://github.com/desktop/desktop/issues/15767) (30), [desktop#5155](https://github.com/desktop/desktop/issues/5155) (26), [sublime_merge#2093](https://github.com/sublimehq/sublime_merge/issues/2093). _Seen in:_ TortoiseGit 2.17.

- [ ] **Undo one file or one hunk of a past commit (S).** In a commit's file list, _Revert changes to this file_. In its diff, _Revert hunk_ or the selected lines. Either one reverse-applies that piece to the working tree, where you can look it over before committing.
  _Asked for:_ [desktop#19207](https://github.com/desktop/desktop/issues/19207) (26), [Fork#333](https://github.com/fork-dev/Tracker/issues/333), [Fork#1280](https://github.com/fork-dev/Tracker/issues/1280).

- [ ] **Graph order and first-parent mode (S).** `--date-order` is hard-coded in `git/commits.rs`. A menu in the graph header would choose topological, date or author-date order. It would also have _First parent only_, which hides the commits a merge brought in and leaves one merge per pull request on main.
  _Asked for:_ [sublime_merge#1169](https://github.com/sublimehq/sublime_merge/issues/1169) (33), [Fork#406](https://github.com/fork-dev/Tracker/issues/406) (15).

- [ ] **"Contained in" in a commit's details (S).** A commit's details list the branches and tags that contain it, and the first release after it (`describe --contains`). They load when the commit is selected.
  _Asked for:_ [sublime_merge#841](https://github.com/sublimehq/sublime_merge/issues/841), [#1211](https://github.com/sublimehq/sublime_merge/issues/1211).

- [ ] **Skip hooks once (S).** Commit and push each get a _Skip hooks_ option (`--no-verify`) that applies to that one run. When a hook fails, the error names the hook.
  _Asked for:_ [Fork#1239](https://github.com/fork-dev/Tracker/issues/1239) (18). _Seen in:_ SourceGit.

- [ ] **The commit message from `prepare-commit-msg`, and completion (S).** The commit box runs the `prepare-commit-msg` hook to prefill the message, as git's own editor would. Typing in the box completes the names of changed files and prefixes used before.
  _Asked for:_ [lazygit#4995](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit/issues/4995), [lazygit#941](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit/issues/941) (19), [sublime_merge#339](https://github.com/sublimehq/sublime_merge/issues/339).

- [ ] **Reset that keeps local changes (S).** `reset --keep` as a fourth kind next to soft, mixed and hard. It moves the branch and stops if that would touch files you've changed.
  _Seen in:_ Sublime Merge 2132.

- [ ] **Detached HEAD in plain words (S).** While HEAD is detached, a banner says "You're looking at an old version; new commits here belong to no branch", with _Create branch here_ and _Back to main_. Checking out something else after committing while detached stops, and offers to keep those commits on a branch. git prints that warning, but a GUI swallows it.

body:
These are ideas for connecting gitcraft to what surrounds git: issue trackers, CI, more forges, accounts and containers. They come from the second round of the idea hunt. They're only suggestions, so take whatever fits and close the rest.

Effort is rough: **S** is a contained addition, **M** a new view or a coordinated flow, **L** new state and integration work.

- [ ] **Start work from an issue (M for one tracker, L for several).** Browse the issues assigned to you on GitHub, GitLab, Forgejo or Gitea, or on Jira or Linear. Pick one and gitcraft makes a branch or a worktree named after it. The issue's acceptance criteria stay in view, and the pull request that follows links back to it.
  _Seen in:_ [GitKraken's Jira integration](https://help.gitkraken.com/gitkraken-desktop/jira/).

- [ ] **Run an Actions workflow locally (M).** Pick a workflow, an event, a job and a matrix entry, then run it against your current changes with an installed [`act`](https://nektosact.com/). The output sits beside the hosted CI runs, and features `act` can't run are named as such.

- [ ] **Full GitLab merge requests (L).** On GitLab, gitcraft only lists and creates merge requests. A merge request would open in the big area like a GitHub pull request does, with its changes, comments on lines, resolving discussions, approval and merging. GitLab's merge blockers would show as well.
  _APIs:_ [merge requests](https://docs.gitlab.com/api/merge_requests/), [discussions](https://docs.gitlab.com/api/discussions/).

- [ ] **Azure DevOps and Bitbucket (L).** New forge providers for listing pull requests, opening one and reviewing it, through `az repos` or REST and Bitbucket's REST API.
  _Asked for:_ the [GitKraken board](https://feedback.gitkraken.com/suggestions/189955/integrated-azure-devops-pull-request-view) (about 70 votes). _Seen in:_ GitButler 0.21 (Bitbucket Cloud).

- [ ] **Each profile with its own SSH key and forge account (S–M).** A profile chooses its SSH key, which goes into its existing `profiles/<id>.gitconfig` as `core.sshCommand`. It also chooses which `gh` / `glab` / `tea` account to use, so a work profile and a personal one push and review as different people. Today a profile only carries the author and signing.
  _Asked for:_ [Fork#1903](https://github.com/fork-dev/Tracker/issues/1903), [Fork#250](https://github.com/fork-dev/Tracker/issues/250).

- [ ] **SSH key helper (S–M).** _Set up SSH_ does four things:
  - makes a key (`ssh-keygen -t ed25519`);
  - adds it to the agent;
  - uploads it to GitHub, Forgejo or Gitea through the forge logins gitcraft already uses;
  - tests it with `ssh -T`.

  For a remote repository this all happens on the remote machine.
  _Seen in:_ SourceGit 2026.19.

- [ ] **Copy a link, or open it on the forge (S).** _Copy link_ and _Open on forge_ for a commit, a file, or a line of a diff, built for all four forges. Today only pull requests and CI runs open in the browser.
  _Asked for:_ [desktop#9791](https://github.com/desktop/desktop/issues/9791), [sublime_merge#900](https://github.com/sublimehq/sublime_merge/issues/900).

- [ ] **Dev containers (L).** gitcraft detects `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` and offers _Start environment_, a terminal inside the container, and a handoff to your editor. It shows which container belongs to which worktree, and explains when one fails to start or rebuild.
  _Seen in:_ the [Dev Container CLI](https://containers.dev/supporting#devcontainer-cli).
title: Ideas: integrations (issue trackers, local CI, more forges, SSH keys, dev containers)

body:
These ideas are for open-source maintainers, release managers, and workflows that don't use pull requests. They came from the second round of the idea hunt. They're only suggestions, so take whatever fits and close the rest.

Effort is rough. **S** means a contained addition, **M** a new view or a coordinated flow, and **L** new state and integration work.

## Maintainers

- [ ] **DCO sign-off (S).**
  - The commit box gets a _Sign off_ toggle.
  - The toggle turns on by itself when a repository has a DCO file or `.github/dco.yml`, or when its DCO check fails.
  - In the pull request view, a failing DCO check offers _Sign off my commits on this branch_. This runs `rebase --signoff` and then a force push with lease, previewed first and undoable.

  Today contributors get a bot reply telling them how to do this in the terminal ([example](https://discuss.gradle.org/t/pull-request-dco-the-sign-off-is-missing/25006)). Other clients have the checkbox, but none fix commits that already exist.

- [ ] **Pull requests from forks (M).**
  - _Push to the contributor's branch_ when the author allows edits from maintainers. It adds the fork as a remote and sets `pushRemote`; today a fork's pull request can only be fetched.
  - _Rebase onto main and push to the contributor_.
  - Badges in the list for _first-time contributor_, _workflows awaiting approval_ (with _Approve and run_) and _maintainers can edit_.

  _Seen in:_ `gh pr checkout`, GitHub Desktop (fork remotes).

- [ ] **CODEOWNERS (S–M).** The owners of each file show on file rows, on a pull request's changed files and on staged changes. A summary says "this branch needs `payments` and `infra`". The _Create pull request_ dialog suggests reviewers from it. It also flags patterns that match nothing and files without an owner.
  _Seen in:_ GitHub and GitLab on the web, [git-codeowners](https://github.com/chazmcgarvey/git-codeowners) (CLI).

## Releases

- [ ] **Cut a release (M).** _Cut release…_ on a commit does the following:
  - suggests the next version from the Conventional Commits since `git describe`;
  - drafts editable release notes grouped by type, with links to the pull requests;
  - makes a signed annotated tag and pushes it;
  - creates the release on the forge, with assets attached (`gh release create`, Gitea / Forgejo's API, `glab`).

  Tag, upload and publish are tracked separately, so a partial failure can be resumed.
  _Seen in:_ [git-cliff](https://git-cliff.org/docs/), release-please, git-extras `git release` (all CLIs). No GUI writes the notes and creates the forge release too.

- [ ] **Hotfix flow (M).** _Start hotfix from v2.3.1_ makes the branch. _Finish hotfix_ tags it, merges it back into main (and develop, if used) and pushes it all, as one step that's previewed and can be undone.
  _Seen in:_ the git-flow buttons of SourceTree, GitKraken and Tower.

- [ ] **What a package will publish (M).** A panel lists the files `cargo package` or `npm pack` would ship. It points out files that are missing or included by accident, and compares them with the published version that's already out.

## Without pull requests

- [ ] **Gerrit (L).** _Push for review_ picks the target branch and a topic, checks the `Change-Id`, and pushes to `refs/for/*`. Commits in the graph link to their Gerrit change, and amending one updates that change's patch set.
  _Docs:_ [Gerrit uploads](https://gerrit-review.googlesource.com/Documentation/user-upload.html).

- [ ] **Patches by email (L).** Paste a public-inbox URL or a Message-ID, and gitcraft fetches the series with `b4`, with its cover letter and review trailers. You can look it over and then apply it. Authors prepare numbered revisions, then preview recipients and the outgoing messages before sending. This goes beyond the patch-file import and export gitcraft already has.
  _Seen in:_ [b4](https://b4.docs.kernel.org/en/latest/index.html).
title: Ideas: maintainers, releases and review without pull requests

body:
Ideas for teams whose repositories are mostly binaries: games, art and data. gitcraft has LFS pointers in diffs, plus _LFS: Fetch_ and _LFS: Pull_. These are from the second round of the idea hunt. They're only suggestions, so take whatever fits and close the rest.

- [ ] **LFS file locks (M).**
  - A padlock on file rows that says who holds the lock and since when ("Locked by Ana · 2 d").
  - _Lock_ and _Unlock_ in a file's menu.
  - An _LFS Locks_ panel that filters, unlocks several at once, and force-unlocks for admins.
  - Changing a lockable file someone else holds warns that the push will be refused.
  - After a push, an offer to unlock what was pushed.

  _Seen in:_ [Fork 1.48 / 1.90](https://fork.dev/releasenoteswin), Sublime Merge build 2125, [Anchorpoint](https://www.anchorpoint.app/blog/using-file-locking-in-git) (a whole product for game teams built around this).

- [ ] **LFS storage and what to download (S–M).** Show how much disk `.git/lfs` takes, and which files are only pointers that were never downloaded (marked in the tree). Also:
  - _Fetch only these folders_ (`lfs.fetchinclude` / `fetchexclude`);
  - _Prune old LFS objects_;
  - _Track \*.psd in LFS_ from a file's menu, which edits `.gitattributes`.

- [ ] **Game engines: Unity first (M).** gitcraft would recognise a Unity project and then:
  - warn when an asset is staged without its `.meta` file, or a `.meta` without its asset (the classic broken-reference bug);
  - offer to register UnityYAMLMerge, with _Solve with UnityYAMLMerge_ in the conflict editor, built like the Mergiraf integration;
  - check that Force Text serialization and `.gitattributes` are set up.

  Unreal could follow.
  _Docs:_ [Unity Smart Merge](https://docs.unity.com/en-us/engine/current/manual/get-started/project-configuration/version-control/smart-merge).

See also the image compare modes, notebooks and tables in the issue on diffs for every kind of file.
title: Ideas: binary-heavy repositories (LFS locks, LFS storage, Unity)

body:
These are ideas for showing a change the right way for each kind of file. Today gitcraft has unified and side-by-side diffs, the changed part of each line marked, images before and after, LFS pointers, and Markdown rendered. They're only suggestions, so take whatever fits and close the rest. These came from the second round of the idea hunt; wave 1 is in #32–#39.

Effort is rough: **S** is a contained addition, **M** is a new view or a coordinated flow, and **L** is substantial rendering or analysis work.

## Code

- [ ] **Moved code (M; L across files).** A block that was deleted in one place and added in another gets a shared "moved" marker and its own muted colour. _Moved to…_ brings the two places together and shows what was edited during the move. git's `--color-moved` already detects this.
  _Seen in:_ [VS Code moved-code detection](https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_82#_moved-code-detection), SmartGit 26.2.

- [ ] **Context that opens where you need it (M).** Between hunks, a fold reads _42 unchanged lines_. It can open upwards or downwards, or as _Show the enclosing function_. Lines you've commented on or selected stay visible. You get more context in one place without switching the whole file to the _File_ view.
  _Seen in:_ VS Code (collapse unchanged regions), GitHub's expand arrows.

- [ ] **Choose the diff algorithm (S).** When a diff pairs lines that have nothing to do with each other, switch between Myers, minimal, patience and histogram right there, keeping your place. A preference can be kept per file type. This sets `DiffOptions` and never changes the repository's config.

- [ ] **Structural diff for refactors (L).** A reading mode that compares syntax, so re-indenting and re-wrapping don't hide the expression that actually changed. It says when a language isn't supported or a file doesn't parse. Staging stays in the normal patch view.
  _Seen in:_ [Difftastic](https://github.com/Wilfred/difftastic).

- [ ] **What did this merge resolve? (M).** On a merge commit, show only what differs between the merge git would have made and the one that was recorded (`git show --remerge-diff`). That reveals the conflict resolutions and any extra edits, which today are lost among everything the merged branch brought in.

- [ ] **Fold generated files and lockfiles (S).** Some files start folded in file lists and diffs, with a line such as _+1,204 −880, generated_:
  - files marked `linguist-generated` or `-diff` in `.gitattributes`;
  - patterns you choose, such as `Cargo.lock` and `*.min.js`.

  _Requested in:_ [sublime_merge#1593](https://github.com/sublimehq/sublime_merge/issues/1593).

- [ ] **Find in a diff, a file or blame (S).** Ctrl+F in the big area highlights matches in the open diff, file or blame, and Enter / Shift+Enter steps through them. Today Ctrl+F only searches commits.
  _Requested in:_ [sublime_merge#429](https://github.com/sublimehq/sublime_merge/issues/429) (47 👍), [#1626](https://github.com/sublimehq/sublime_merge/issues/1626), [#512](https://github.com/sublimehq/sublime_merge/issues/512).

- [ ] **File migration map (M).** When a change reorganises folders, show the old folders on the left and the new ones on the right, joined by ribbons for the renames and copies, each with git's similarity score. Clicking a ribbon shows only the edits made to the content, separate from the move.

## Text and documents

- [ ] **Prose mode: wrapping and word changes (S–M).** In `.md`, `.adoc`, `.rst` and `.txt`, a paragraph is often one long line, and the diff doesn't wrap it. Prose mode would:
  - wrap long lines;
  - mark the words that changed, even when the paragraph was re-wrapped;
  - add a wrap switch to every diff.

  _Requested in:_ [desktop#11052](https://github.com/desktop/desktop/issues/11052) (42 👍, wrap). _Like:_ `git diff --word-diff`, [wdiff](https://www.gnu.org/software/wdiff/).

- [ ] **Documents and binaries (S–M).** Instead of "Binary files differ":
  - SVGs show as images before and after, with a switch to their code (`image_fit.rs` can already load them);
  - `.docx`, `.pdf` and `.odt` show as text, through the user's `textconv` or pandoc when installed;
  - archives list their members;
  - other files show their sizes and a hex view of both sides.

  _Seen in:_ TortoiseGit 2.15 (SVG), SourceGit (hex), [diffoscope](https://diffoscope.org/). _Requested in:_ [desktop#11316](https://github.com/desktop/desktop/issues/11316).

- [ ] **Image compare modes and a filmstrip (S–M).** The image diff gets four modes, 2-up, Swipe, Onion skin and Difference. Zoom and pan stay linked across them, the size and dimensions change is shown, and transparency gets a checkerboard. An image's file history becomes a strip of thumbnails.
  _Seen in:_ [GitHub image view modes](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/using-files/working-with-non-code-files#viewing-differences).

## Data and configuration

- [ ] **Notebooks (M–L).** `.ipynb` files diff cell by cell. The source is shown, outputs (images included) are rendered before and after, and execution counts and metadata are folded away. There is optionally _Strip outputs when committing_ (a clean filter, like nbstripout). Notebook-aware conflicts come later, and cells are never executed.
  _Seen in:_ [nbdime](https://nbdime.readthedocs.io/) (web and CLI, no desktop client).

- [ ] **Tables, and DVC (M).** CSV and TSV files diff as a grid of added, removed and changed rows and cells, with renamed columns detected. `.dvc` files show the data they track (size, hash, path), as LFS pointers already do, and the palette gets _DVC: Pull_.
  _Like:_ daff, the DVC VS Code extension.

- [ ] **Config files by key (M).** JSON, YAML and TOML can switch to a key-path view such as `server.timeout: 30 → 60`, with added and removed keys and changed types. Reordered keys are told apart from changed values. A click goes back to the line.
  _Seen in:_ [dyff](https://github.com/homeport/dyff).

- [ ] **Dependency changes (L).** A change to `Cargo.lock` or `package-lock.json` becomes a list of packages: upgraded, added and removed. Each has links to its registry page and changelog, and changes of licence are shown.
  _Seen in:_ [GitHub Dependency Review](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/tutorials/secure-your-dependencies/customize-dependency-review-action).

- [ ] **API contract changes (M).** When an OpenAPI spec changes, list the breaking changes: removed endpoints, parameters that became required, narrowed responses. Each one opens its place in the file.
  _Seen in:_ [oasdiff](https://www.oasdiff.com/).

- [ ] **Encrypted files (M).** SOPS files are recognised. _Show decrypted_ compares them through the user's own `sops` and keys, and tells a change of recipients or keys apart from a change of content. The plain text is never cached.
  _Seen in:_ [SOPS](https://getsops.io/docs/).
title: Ideas: diffs for every kind of file (moved code, prose, notebooks, images, config, dependencies)

body:
Accessibility in gitcraft: keyboard focus, contrast and screen readers. I found these while going through the code and `ui_shot` screenshots, and they're suggestions only, so take whatever fits and close the rest.

- [ ] **Visible keyboard focus (S–M).** Pressing Tab three times in the repository view shows no focus ring at all. About 78 hand-painted widgets use `allocate_exact_size` / `interact` with `Sense::click()` alone: palette rows, pills, home cards and file rows. They either can't take focus or don't show it. A shared helper should make them focusable and draw an accent ring while `has_focus()`.

- [ ] **Contrast (S).** I measured these in `src/theme.rs`. Each one is below WCAG AA's 4.5:1 for small text:
  - `text_faint` on `card` is 3.2:1 in Dark, 2.9:1 in Medium Gray and 3.9:1 in Light. That colour is used for the 10.5 px section headers (LOCAL, RECENT, the manual's headings).
  - White on `accent` (the checked-out pill, the primary buttons) is 3.3:1.

  Raising the faint and accent tokens would fix these. A High-contrast theme could also go next to the PhotoCraft ones.

- [ ] **Screen-reader labels (S–M).** `Cargo.toml` turns on egui's `accesskit` feature, but only `spinner.rs` calls `widget_info`. Pills, graph rows, palette rows, file rows and the home cards all reach screen readers without a label. A `widgets::a11y(resp, WidgetType, label)` helper would cover every hand-painted widget. A graph row would then read "commit a301da9, Merge…, Jonas, 26 minutes ago, branch dev".

- [ ] **A graph you can hear (M).** With a screen reader, the arrow keys would follow lanes (parent, child, next merge, branch tip) instead of rows. gitcraft would describe the shape of the history, not just the text, for example _feature/login, 3 ahead and 12 behind main, branched 2 days ago, merged into release once_. Optional short sounds would mark lane crossings and merges. This needs a lane-walking mode in `repo/navigate.rs`, AccessKit descriptions for each row, and `rodio` for the sounds.
  _Closest:_ [BranchFlow](https://codeberg.org/colabottles/branchflow), a young web project. I found no desktop git GUI that describes its graph in words.

- [ ] **Respect the system's reduced-motion setting** for the animations in the UI ideas issue, and for the tab slide that exists today.
title: Ideas: accessibility (focus, contrast, screen readers)

body:
These are UI and UX ideas from a pass over the code and over headless screenshots made with `examples/ui_shot.rs` on gitcraft's own repository. They're only suggestions, so take whatever fits and close the rest. Accessibility is in its own issue.

Effort is rough: **S** is a contained change, **M** a new view or a coordinated flow, **L** a larger rework.

## Quick wins

- [ ] **Ranked palette results with the matches highlighted (S).** `fuzzy()` in `app/palette.rs` only checks that the letters appear in order, and results keep their list order. So typing `reb` shows _Pull (rebase)_ and _Create branch_ first and _Rebase dev onto…_ last. Instead:
  - score each match (word starts, consecutive letters, prefix) and sort by the score;
  - put recently used entries on top;
  - draw the matched letters in the accent colour.

  _Seen in:_ VS Code, Raycast, Zed.

- [ ] **Shortcuts for the main actions and for tabs (S).** A repository tab only handles Esc, Ctrl+Z/Y, Ctrl+F and F7 (`repo/layout.rs`). There are no keys for Fetch, Pull, Push, Stash, New branch, Terminal or Stage all, and no Ctrl+Tab or Ctrl+1…9 to switch tabs. The shortcuts should also show in the toolbar's tooltips and in the palette, where the hint is a category ("remote", "branch") today.

- [ ] **A graph that reads better (S).**
  - The Description column ends up about 120 px wide, while the Branch / Tag column takes about 260 px and is mostly empty. Give Description the flexible width, and let the ref column shrink when no pill is in view.
  - Summaries are cut hard with no ellipsis (`row.rs` uses a clip rect): "fix: CodeRabbit on f". Add an ellipsis and a tooltip with the whole message.
  - Lanes that have commits but no ref in view read as orphans. Give them a faint label, the ref's name or _detached_.

- [ ] **Start page that does more (S–M).** `app/home.rs` shows four cards and a plain recent list. Add:
  - type to filter, ↑ / ↓ and Enter to open;
  - each recent repository's branch, a dot when it has uncommitted changes, and when it was last opened;
  - a dropped folder opens it, and a dropped `.patch` applies it (nothing handles `dropped_files` today);
  - _Scan a folder for repositories_.

- [ ] **Shortcuts and reasons inside context menus (S).** Context menus have no icons or shortcut labels. Greyed-out items such as _Drop commit_ give their reason only on hover. Show the reason in small text under the item instead.

- [ ] **The start page's card subtitles nearly touch the card borders (S).** One example is "An existing local repository".

## Medium

- [ ] **Drag and drop in the graph and the sidebar (M).**
  - Drag a branch's pill onto another pill, a commit or a sidebar branch, and a small menu offers _Merge x into y_, _Rebase y onto x_, _Interactive rebase_ and _Fast-forward_.
  - Drag a commit onto the HEAD pill to cherry-pick it.
  - Drag commits of the current branch to reorder them, or onto another commit to squash.
  - Valid targets light up while dragging.

  egui has `dnd_drag_source` and `dnd_drop_zone`, and the rewrite code of the quick edits already exists. This is the interaction people mention most about GitKraken.
  _Seen in:_ [Tower drag and drop](https://git-tower.com/features/drag-and-drop) (Alt to rebase), GitKraken, [Fork 2.55](https://fork.dev/releasenotes).

- [ ] **Keyboard-first staging and moving between panes (M).**
  - Ctrl+1/2/3 focus the sidebar, the graph and the right pane.
  - In file lists, j / k move, Space stages or unstages, and Enter opens the diff.
  - In a diff, S / U / D act on the current hunk.

  Staging is mouse-only today.
  _Seen in:_ Sublime Merge, lazygit.

- [ ] **A palette that knows what's selected (M).** `palette_items` adds about six entries per local branch (Compare ×2, Merge, Rebase, Check out, Push), which floods the results in a large repository, and it has nothing for the selected commit. Two changes:
  - put actions for the selection on top: _Cherry-pick a301da9_, _Revert_, _Reset dev to here…_;
  - two steps instead of one entry per combination: pick the verb, then the branch.

  _Seen in:_ [Raycast's action panel](https://manual.raycast.com/action-panel).

- [ ] **A diff beside the graph, and back / forward (M).** Opening a diff replaces the graph, and Esc is the only way back. There is no history across graph → diff → file history → blame. Add an optional split, with the graph on top and the diff below, and Alt+← / Alt+→ through the recent views.

- [ ] **Guided empty states and tips in context (S–M).** A repository with no commits only says "No commits yet" in the toolbar. Several features are only explained in the manual: Ctrl+click to compare, double-click a pill, Solo. Add:
  - an empty graph that offers _Make the first commit_, _Add a remote_ and _Publish_;
  - one "Did you know" line, drawn from the manual's features, that can be dismissed;
  - a hint the first time a related action happens: _Tip: Ctrl+click another commit to compare_.

## Bigger

- [ ] **One action registry, rebindable keys, chords and a "which-key" overlay (L).** Settings → Keyboard shortcuts is a read-only list built from `manual::SHORTCUTS`, and shortcuts are handled in three hard-coded places. One registry of actions would drive the manual, the palette, the tooltips, the menus and the handlers. It would allow rebinding and chords such as Ctrl+K …, with an overlay of the keys that can follow while a chord is pending.
  _Seen in:_ [Zed key bindings](https://zed.dev/docs/key-bindings), Emacs which-key.

- [ ] **Pop panels out to another window (L).** There's one viewport. With egui's multi-viewport support (`show_viewport_deferred`), _Pop out_ would move the diff, the terminal, a pull request or the CI view to a second monitor. Dragging a tab out of the strip would give it its own window.

- [ ] **Motion that explains what changed (M–L).** After a fetch, pull or rebase the graph simply jumps. Instead:
  - incoming commits light up briefly and get a _new_ marker after a fetch;
  - pills slide to their new commit after a merge, reset or rebase;
  - the graph scrolls smoothly to HEAD.

  All of it follows the system's reduced-motion setting. `animate_value` is only used for sliding tabs today.
title: Ideas: UI / UX polish (palette, keyboard, drag and drop, feedback)

body:
These are features that Tower, Fork, Sublime Merge, SmartGit, GitKraken, GitHub Desktop, Git Extensions and Magit have and gitcraft doesn't yet. They're everyday conveniences and power-user tools, not new ideas. They're only suggestions, so take whatever fits and close the rest.

I checked each one against the README, the manual and `src/`. Effort is rough: **S** is a contained addition, **M** a new view or a coordinated flow, **L** new state and recovery work.

## Most useful

- [ ] **Commit templates, Conventional Commits and co-authors (S).**
  - The commit box starts from the repository's `commit.template`. Git only fills that in for its own editor, so gitcraft has to load it itself.
  - Saved templates.
  - An optional type / scope picker (Conventional Commits, Gitmoji).
  - _Add co-author_ picks from the repository's authors and writes a `Co-authored-by:` trailer.
  - Issue references such as `JIRA-12` in messages become links.

  _Seen in:_ [Tower commit templates](https://www.git-tower.com/commit-templates), [GitKraken](https://help.gitkraken.com/gitkraken-desktop/commits/), GitHub Desktop (co-authors).

- [ ] **Branch cleanup (S–M).** _Merged_ and _Stale_ badges on the sidebar's branches. _Select stale or merged branches…_ deletes them in one go, here and on the remote. Detection uses:
  - `git branch --merged`;
  - `git cherry`, for work that was rebased;
  - the merged pull requests gitcraft already lists, which catch squash merges.

  _Seen in:_ [Tower 15 / 17](https://www.git-tower.com/release-notes/mac), Fork 2.62 (_Select Stale Local Branches_).

- [ ] **Stash only some files, or only the staged ones; snapshot (S).** _Stash selected files_ runs `git stash push -- <paths>`, _Stash staged_ runs `--staged`, and _Snapshot_ saves a stash but leaves the working tree as it is.
  _Seen in:_ Tower (partial stash, snapshots).

- [ ] **AI commit message through a CLI you already have (S–M).** A button in the commit box sends the staged diff to `claude -p`, `codex exec`, `gh copilot` or a command you set, and fills in the message. _Review this branch_ does the same with what a branch adds to main. gitcraft stores no API key and uses the tools that are already installed, just as it does for `gh` and `glab`.
  _Seen in:_ GitKraken 11, [GitHub Desktop 3.5](https://github.blog/changelog/2025-06-24-github-desktop-3-5-github-copilot-commit-message-generation-now-generally-available), Tower 16, Fork 2.59–2.70 (Claude, Codex), SmartGit 25.1.

- [ ] **External diff and merge tools (S–M).** _Open in diff tool_ on files and _Resolve in merge tool_ on conflicts. They use the configured `diff.tool` / `merge.tool` (Beyond Compare, Araxis, VS Code, Meld) or a preset, and the view refreshes when the tool closes. This works locally and on WSL through `\\wsl.localhost`. Over SSH the tool has to be on that machine.
  _Seen in:_ [Fork](https://fork.dev/releasenoteswin), [SmartGit](https://docs.syntevo.com/SmartGit/Latest/HowTos/), Tower.

- [ ] **Custom commands (M).** Settings → Custom commands. Each one has:
  - a name;
  - where it shows up (a commit's, a branch's or a file's menu, or the palette);
  - a command line with `$SHA`, `$BRANCH`, `$FILE` and `$REPO` in it.

  It can ask for a text or a branch first, runs on the repository's machine, and its output goes to the terminal or a toast.
  _Seen in:_ Fork (`custom-commands.json`, with prompts), Tower 12 (custom workflows), lazygit custom commands.

## Smaller

- [ ] **Clone options: shallow, partial and sparse (S–M).** The clone dialog offers depth, blobless (`--filter=blob:none`) and the folders to check out. Later a folder-tree picker would edit an open repository's sparse-checkout, and say when reading an old file has to download objects.
  _Seen in:_ GitKraken 11.8 / 11.10, [Magit sparse checkouts](https://docs.magit.vc/magit/Sparse-checkouts.html).

- [ ] **Why is this file ignored? (M).** In a file's menu, this shows the rule responsible (`git check-ignore -v`). Also shown: the file's effective attributes (end of line, text or binary, LFS, merge driver, from `git check-attr -a`). Its rules can be edited, with a preview of the files a change would affect. This helps with CRLF churn, files that seem to vanish, and merge drivers that don't run.
  _Seen in:_ [Git Extensions](https://git-extensions-documentation.readthedocs.io/en/main/maintenance.html#ignore-files) (ignore editor only).

- [ ] **Hooks (M).** A page that shows:
  - the hooks folder in effect;
  - which hooks are active and which operations run them;
  - problems such as a hook that isn't executable or has CRLF line endings;
  - each hook's output, readable after it ran.

  It also recognises hook managers (husky, lefthook, pre-commit). Installing hooks can come later.
  _Seen in:_ [GitTree](https://gittree.app/en/docs/desktop/changes/git-hooks).

- [ ] **Repository health and maintenance (M).** A page that shows:
  - object counts and sizes;
  - how long the last loads took;
  - what could speed things up: the commit-graph, `git maintenance start`, fsmonitor, untracked cache.

  Each of these can be turned on with one click. Browsing a million-commit history also needs the 100 000-commit limit and the graph rebuild looked at.
  _Seen in:_ [Git Extensions](https://git-extensions-documentation.readthedocs.io/en/main/maintenance.html), [SmartGit performance tuning](https://docs.syntevo.com/SmartGit/24.1/HowTos/Performance-Tuning).

- [ ] **Bundles (S–M).** Export chosen refs or a range to a `git bundle`, and check and look into an incoming one before importing its refs. This is for machines without network access, support handoffs and backups.
  _Seen in:_ [Magit](https://docs.magit.vc/magit/Bundle.html).

- [ ] **Scrub history with filter-repo (L).** A separate cleanup flow: pick paths or replacements, rewrite a fresh clone with `git filter-repo`, report the refs it changed, and check the result. Publishing it is its own step, with a reminder that a leaked secret also has to be revoked.
  _Benchmark:_ [git-filter-repo](https://github.com/newren/git-filter-repo/blob/main/Documentation/git-filter-repo.txt).

- [ ] **Workspaces (L).** Named groups of repositories. The start page shows a dashboard for each group, with every repository's branch, uncommitted files, ahead / behind and last fetch. _Fetch all_ and _Open all_ work on a whole group. Bulk pull can come later, because handling its failures is harder.
  _Seen in:_ [GitKraken Workspaces](https://help.gitkraken.com/gitkraken-desktop/workspaces/), Fork 2.71, Tower (repository groups).
title: Ideas: everyday git features other clients have

body:
Ideas for understanding a repository through its history: why a line is the way it is, where a function went, and what usually changes together. gitcraft already has file history (which follows renames), blame, `log -S` code search, and a view of the whole file at a commit. These go further. They are only suggestions, so take whatever fits and close the rest.

Effort is rough: **S** is a contained addition, **M** a new view or a coordinated flow, **L** new state and recovery work.

## Most useful

- [ ] **History of selected lines (S).** Select lines in a file or a diff, then pick _History of these lines_. It lists every commit that touched them (`git log -L`) and opens in the existing file-history pane.
  _Seen in:_ [Fork 2.59](https://fork.dev/releasenotes), JetBrains' "Show History for Selection".

- [ ] **Search operators (S–M).** The Ctrl+F field would understand these operators:
  - `author:`, `path:`, `after:` and `before:`
  - `contents:` (`-S`) and `regex:` (`-G`)
  - `merges:`

  They map to `git log` options and combine with each other. Typing an operator brings up suggestions for it, such as authors and paths.
  _Seen in:_ [Sublime Merge](https://www.sublimemerge.com/docs/search).

- [ ] **Signature verification (M).** A commit's details would show its signature as valid, invalid, unknown key, unsigned or not checked, together with the signer and git's output. Verification happens when a commit is selected; badges on the visible rows can be cached. History loading turns signature checks off on purpose, and that should stay.
  _Seen in:_ [Sublime Merge](https://www.sublimemerge.com/download), [Git Extensions](https://git-extensions-documentation.readthedocs.io/en/main/browse_repository.html#gpg).

- [ ] **Saved views of the graph (M).** Presets such as these:
  - _My unpushed work_
  - _My recent changes and what they depend on_
  - _Descendants of this commit_
  - _Only merges into main_

  Long runs of history in between collapse into a connector you can expand. They pick commits by how they relate to each other, which hiding or soloing branches can't do. They would be built on git revision queries rather than a new query language.
  _Seen in:_ [Sapling ISL](https://sapling-scm.com/docs/addons/isl/), [jj revsets](https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/revsets/), [jjui](https://github.com/idursun/jjui).

- [ ] **Git notes (S).** A _Notes_ section in a commit's details to add, edit and delete notes, with the namespace chosen. A notes namespace can be fetched or pushed explicitly. Notes attach findings, review context or build links to a commit without rewriting it.
  _Seen in:_ [Git Extensions](https://git-extensions-documentation.readthedocs.io/en/main/notes.html).

## Bigger

- [ ] **Line dossier: why is this line like this? (M–L).** Right-click a line and pick _Explain history_. A card shows every version of the line, following it through moves and reformatting (`blame -w -C -C -M`, repeated on each commit's parent). Each version shows its commit and the pull request that brought it in. The card also shows **the review comments that were made on those lines in that pull request**, and the linked issue. An optional LLM summary, run on your own key or a local model, cites each card. gitcraft can offer to add formatting-only commits to `.git-blame-ignore-revs`.
  _Closest:_ GitLens line history and its pull-request hovers, which only work on GitHub and don't show review comments.

- [ ] **Symbol biography (L).** Pick a function and see its life on a timeline like a video editor's: when it was created, renamed, moved to another file, split and deleted. Scrubbing the timeline steps its body through each version, with the author and pull request of each step. A symbol is found by name with tree-sitter, and by how similar its body is across files linked by rename detection.
  _Closest:_ `git log -L :func:file`, which loses the function once it moves to another file.

- [ ] **What usually comes with this? (M).** While you stage a change to the serializer, gitcraft notices: _changes like this usually also touch the compatibility fixtures, and those haven't changed_. A click shows the past commits behind the hint. It counts which files change together, leaving out bulk and generated commits. Every hint can be dismissed and shows its evidence.
  _Closest:_ [CodeScene's change coupling](https://codescene.io/docs/guides/technical/change-coupling.html), a hosted analysis that doesn't help while you stage.
title: Ideas: understanding a repository's history

body:
Ideas for reviewing pull requests in gitcraft. gitcraft already shows a pull request in full on GitHub, Forgejo and Gitea, and lets you comment, review, reply, apply suggestions and merge. These go beyond that. They are only suggestions, so take whatever fits and close the rest.

Effort is rough. **S** is a contained addition, **M** a new view or a coordinated flow, **L** new state and recovery work, and **XL** a project of its own.

## Most useful

- [ ] **What changed since I last looked (M).** gitcraft remembers which head of a pull request you reviewed. After the author force-pushes, a banner says _rewritten: 2 commits changed, 1 added, 3 identical_. Clicking it shows a diff of the diffs, pairing old and new commits with `git range-diff`. Your earlier line comments move forward onto the matching new lines. GitHub's "changes since last review" breaks on force pushes ([discussion](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/3478)), and Forgejo and Gitea have nothing like it.
  _Closest:_ the `git range-diff` CLI, and [GitButler's write-up](https://blog.gitbutler.com/interdiff-review-with-git-range-diff).

- [ ] **One continuous review page (M).** _Review all changes_ scrolls through every changed file as one document, with file headers you can fold and hunk actions in place. It would work for the working tree, a commit, a comparison or a pull request, which matters for refactors that touch many files. Being able to edit working-tree hunks right there could come later.
  _Seen in:_ [Zed's project diff](https://zed.dev/docs/git#project-diff), [VS Code's multi-diff editor](https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_86).

- [ ] **A pull-request inbox across repositories (M–L).** One list of the pull requests that wait for your review, or are yours and have new comments or failing checks, across every repository you've opened and every forge. A click opens the pull request in its tab.
  _Seen in:_ [GitKraken Launchpad](https://www.gitkraken.com/features/launchpad) (Pro).

## Bigger

- [ ] **Review freshness (L).** Come back to a rewritten pull request and see three kinds of change:
  - unchanged since you reviewed;
  - changed directly;
  - unchanged text whose dependencies changed, for example "this caller didn't change, but its callee now returns a different error".

  The exact parts (blobs, patches) come first. Dependencies would follow through tree-sitter or a language server, one language at a time.
  _Closest:_ [Reviewable's per-file review state](https://docs.reviewable.io/files).

- [ ] **Reviewer echo (M).** gitcraft builds a small personal rulebook from the review comments you have written on all forges. Before you push, it checks your outgoing diff against it: _you'd flag this: you asked for no `unwrap()` in handlers_, with a link to your own comment. It runs with your own API key or a local model, and it's opt-in.
  _Closest:_ [cubic](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/ai-that-learns-your-team-s-unwritten-rules), which is hosted, team-wide and works only on pull requests.

- [ ] **AI objections that come with a reproducer (L).** Instead of an AI review that says "this might break Unicode", ask it to _Show me_. A model writes a small test, gitcraft runs it against the base and the head, and puts the observed difference next to the hunk. The judgement that the change is wrong stays with the person. Start with one ecosystem, such as Rust unit tests, and run the generated code in a sandbox.

- [ ] **Review storyboard (M–L).** The author arranges a pull request into a short sequence: the old failure, the invariant, the fix, the result. Each card opens a pinned hunk, a file at a commit, or a test result. When new pushes change what a card points at, the card is marked stale. It's stored with base and head IDs, and the anchors survive rebases through range-diff.
  _Closest:_ [CodeTour](https://github.com/microsoft/codetour), which isn't tied to revisions.

- [ ] **Fix survival radar (L).** Pin an important fix and see where it stands on each release branch:
  - same patch found (patch-id);
  - adapted version linked;
  - regression test passes;
  - not checked.

  A later revert turns a branch amber. "The patch is there" is kept apart from "the behaviour was tested".
  _Closest:_ [Tower's merged-PR detection](https://www.git-tower.com/pro/pr-merged-detection) answers a different question, whether a pull request was merged.

- [ ] **Backport by contract (L).** Drag a fix onto an older release and give its intended behaviour as a regression test. gitcraft cherry-picks it in a scratch worktree for each target and tells _patch applied_ apart from _test passes_. Any adaptation shows next to the original.
  _Closest:_ [cherry-picker](https://github.com/python/cherry-picker), [Boro](https://github.com/nvidia/boro).

- [ ] **Intent cards (M–L).** Before you start, post a short, expiring note such as _changing token lifetime, until 15:00_ on a path or a symbol. Teammates using gitcraft see it next to that code before any commit exists. It travels through a small git ref of its own, never acts as a lock, and shows stale or offline as such.
  _Closest:_ [Heddle's intent leases](https://github.com/zyads/heddle), [GitKraken's overlap warnings](https://help.gitkraken.com/gitkraken-desktop/conflict-prevention/).

- [ ] **Release choreography across repositories (XL).** Put the backend, the SDK and the frontend on one board, and state a rule such as _the backend supports both protocols before the SDK switches_. gitcraft rehearses the in-between combinations and works out which release order keeps everything compatible. Planning and tests come first. Publishing comes later and needs its own coordination, since separate servers can't push atomically together.
