body:
These are ideas for tests, bisect and the remote-machine side of gitcraft. gitcraft can already run git on WSL and SSH machines, keep several shells open there and make worktrees. Few other clients can do either, so here is what could be built on top. They are only suggestions: take whatever fits and close the rest.

Effort is rough. **S** is a contained addition, **M** a new view or a coordinated flow, **L** new state and recovery work, and **XL** a project of its own.

## Most useful

- [ ] **Bisect (M).** _Start bisect_ from a commit's menu. A banner then offers _Good_, _Bad_ and _Skip_ and says how many steps are left, and the graph colours the good and bad commits. At the end it shows the culprit and puts the checkout back. A bisect started in the terminal is picked up and can be continued. Later, an optional _Run this command_ mode does `git bisect run`.
  _Seen in:_ [Fork 2.56](https://fork.dev/releasenotes) (good / bad colours), [Magit](https://docs.magit.vc/magit/Bisecting.html).

- [ ] **Parallel bisect on a bigger machine (L).** Mark good and bad, type a test command, and choose _run on build-host (32 cores)_. gitcraft splits the range k ways and tests k commits at once, each in its own worktree on that machine. That takes about log_k(n) rounds instead of log₂(n). The graph rows turn green or red as results come in, and the range visibly shrinks. gitcraft picks the commits itself (`git rev-list --bisect-all`), runs one worktree per pooled shell, and stores the results by tree.
  _Closest:_ nothing shipped; it has been [asked for on the git list](https://public-inbox.org/git/012301d67289$c5c36010$514a2030$@nexbridge.com/T/).

- [ ] **Test lane (M).** An optional graph column shows a pass / fail dot per commit for a command you choose, for example `cargo test`, run on the repository's machine. _Test my branch_ fills it in the background, in throwaway worktrees, so you can keep working. Results are keyed by tree, so a rebase that leaves a commit's tree as it was keeps its dot. They are stored in git notes in the same format as git-test, so the CLI shares the cache. This catches a commit in the middle of a branch that doesn't build even though the tip does.
  _Seen in:_ [git-test](https://github.com/mhagger/git-test), [git-branchless test](https://github.com/arxanas/git-branchless/wiki/Command:-git-test) (both CLIs).

- [ ] **Where's my work? (S–M).** One panel looks through every repository gitcraft knows, on every machine (recent ones, WSL distributions, `~/.ssh/config` hosts), and lists:
  - commits not pushed;
  - stashes;
  - worktrees with uncommitted changes;
  - branches whose remote branch is gone.

  Each row has _Push_ and _Open_. It costs one shell round trip per repository, done on the background pools.
  _Closest:_ [git-scan](https://github.com/johnaparker/git-scan), a CLI that hasn't been updated since 2019.

## Bigger

- [ ] **Teleport (M).** Drag a tab onto another machine, for example from the laptop to the build server or from Windows to WSL. The branch, the staged and unstaged changes and the untracked files arrive there in a new worktree, and a tab opens on it. No push, forge or cloud is involved. A snapshot is taken through a temporary index (`write-tree`, `commit-tree`), so nothing of yours is touched. It travels as a `git bundle` through the open shell (`base64 -d` is already required there) and is unpacked into a new worktree on the other machine.
  _Closest:_ VS Code's "Continue Working On", which needs an account and Microsoft's service.

- [ ] **Same code, different machines (L).** Link the local, WSL and SSH copies of a project. gitcraft then says something like _the tracked files match; Linux passes, Windows fails_, and expanding that shows why: case collisions, executable bits, line endings, tool versions, chosen git settings. It only ever collects facts from an allowlist, never environment variables or credentials.

- [ ] **Agent worktrees (M).** _Start agent task…_ makes a branch and a worktree, then opens a terminal tab there running the agent CLI you pick (`claude`, `codex`, …). A panel lists the running ones with their uncommitted changes, and each one's result can be reviewed with the normal diff.
  _Seen in:_ GitKraken 12 Agent Mode, SmartGit 26.2 preview, Fork 2.60.

- [ ] **Find the combination that breaks (L).** Two branches each pass on their own but fail together. _Find the interaction_ tests subsets of their commits in isolated checkouts until it can say "these two commits fail together; either alone passes". It has a budget, and re-runs results that look flaky. This is delta debugging (`ddmin`) applied to integrating branches.

- [ ] **Behaviour timeline (L–XL).** Scrub through commits like frames in a video editor and watch something change across them: a command's output, a benchmark number, a rendered screenshot. Click the first frame where it changes to see the commit. Results are cached by tree, command and machine. Results that were never run, or don't repeat the same, are marked as such and never filled in by guessing.
title: Ideas: tests, bisect and the remote machines

body:
These ideas are about reshaping commits after the fact and keeping a stack of dependent branches in order. That's where tools such as jj, Sapling, GitButler, Graphite, git-branchless, lazygit and Magit are ahead. They're only suggestions, so take whatever fits and close the rest.

I left out what gitcraft already has: interactive rebase, quick edits (edit message, drop, move up or down), staging lines and undo. Effort is rough. **S** is a contained addition, **M** a new view or a coordinated flow, and **L** needs new state and recovery work.

## Most useful

- [ ] **Fold staged changes into an older commit (S).** Stage a review fix, pick the commit it belongs to in the graph (or next to _Amend_), and choose _Fold staged changes into this commit_. Before anything runs, it shows the target and the descendants that will be rewritten. Then it makes a `fixup!` commit and autosquashes it. Keeping the `fixup!` for later should also be possible. The rebase editor can already mark a commit as a fixup, but it can't send today's staged changes to an older commit.
  _Seen in:_ [Magit instant fixup](https://docs.magit.vc/magit/Creating-a-new-commit.html), [lazygit amend an old commit](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit#amend-an-old-commit).

- [ ] **What changed between two versions of a branch (M).** After a rebase, or when a pull request is force-pushed, _Compare versions_ shows the old series and the new one side by side:
  - commits that didn't change fade out;
  - changed, added and dropped commits stand out;
  - clicking a pair shows how its patch changed.

  This is `git range-diff`. gitcraft's compare shows how two trees differ, not how a patch series changed. Keep the old base and tip of every rewrite so _compare before / after_ is always one click away.
  _Seen in:_ [git range-diff](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-range-diff), [magit-tbdiff](https://github.com/magit/magit-tbdiff).

- [ ] **Split a commit (M).** Choose _Split commit…_ and assign its files, hunks or lines to two (later more) new commits, each with its own message. Check both patches, then the descendants are replayed. The line selection of `repo/diff/select.rs` and the rewrite code already exist.
  _Seen in:_ [lazygit custom patches](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit#rebase-magic-custom-patches), [Sapling split](https://sapling-scm.com/docs/overview/stacks/), [GitUp](https://gitup.co/), [GitKraken Commit Composer](https://gitkraken.com/blog/gitkraken-desktop-11-3-ai-powered-commit-cleanup-without-the-chaos) (which also suggests the split with AI).

- [ ] **Remember conflict resolutions (S–M).** A per-repository switch for `git rerere`. When it reuses a resolution, the conflict editor says so and shows what it reused, which you can check or forget (`rerere forget`). The result stays unstaged until you've looked at it. Mergiraf reasons about the syntax; this reuses a decision you already made.
  _Seen in:_ [GitTree](https://gittree.app/en/docs/desktop/integration/reuse-conflict-resolutions).

## Stacked branches

- [ ] **Branches that depend on branches (M).** _This branch is based on…_ records a parent, for example in `branch.<x>.gitcraft-parent`, and suggests one from ancestry. The sidebar and graph then show `main → schema → api → ui` as a stack. Each layer shows its own changes, its parent, its pull request, and whether it needs restacking.
  _Seen in:_ [Graphite](https://graphite.com/docs/restack-branches), [Git Town](https://www.git-town.com/commands/sync), [GitButler stacks](https://docs.gitbutler.com/overview), [Tower 12](https://www.git-tower.com/release-notes/mac).

- [ ] **Restack after an edit (M–L).** After a lower branch changes, show _3 dependent branches need updating_ and preview their new bases. They are then replayed in order, and a stop on conflicts can be resumed. One undo puts every branch back. The interactive rebase gets an _Update dependent branches_ box (`--update-refs`) for the simple case, but `--update-refs` skips branches that are checked out in worktrees.
  _Seen in:_ [git-branchless](https://github.com/arxanas/git-branchless), [Sapling restack](https://sapling-scm.com/docs/commands/restack/), Fork 2.61.

- [ ] **Publish and update a stack of pull requests (L).** Preview each pull request's base and patch, then publish them bottom-up. Later, update them all together. When a lower one merges, retarget the ones above it. Partial success is recorded, so a retry doesn't create duplicates. This works on all four forges, since gitcraft already creates pull requests on each.
  _Seen in:_ [Graphite](https://graphite.com/), [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack), [spr](https://github.com/ejoffe/spr).

## Bigger

- [ ] **Absorb (M).** _Distribute staged fixes_ suggests which earlier commit of the branch each staged hunk belongs to. Accept the clear ones, change the rest, and anything without a match stays staged. It can run an installed `git-absorb` (on the repository's machine for WSL / SSH) before gitcraft has its own.
  _Seen in:_ [git-absorb](https://github.com/tummychow/git-absorb), [Sapling absorb](https://sapling-scm.com/docs/commands/absorb/).

- [ ] **Move hunks between commits (L).** Select a hunk in a commit and choose _Move to commit…_ or _Move back to working changes_. It previews the hunk leaving one commit and arriving in the other, then rewrites the range. This extends _Split commit_.
  _Seen in:_ lazygit custom patches, [GG](https://github.com/gulbanana/gg).

- [ ] **Drag to reorder in the interactive rebase (S–M).** The rebase list moves commits with up / down buttons today. Add drag handles, and P / R / S / F / D keys to set a row's action. Fork also lets you reorder or squash by dragging in the graph itself (see the UI issue).
  _Seen in:_ [GitKraken interactive rebase](https://help.gitkraken.com/gitkraken-client/interactive-rebase), [egui_dnd](https://docs.rs/egui_dnd).

- [ ] **Conflict decisions that remember why (M).** When you resolve a conflict, you can add a note ("keep the new validation, keep the old wire format") and a test command. Next time the same conflict comes back, gitcraft offers that decision with its reason and says whether the test still passes. If the code around it changed, the decision is shown as stale instead of applied quietly. This is rerere with the reasoning attached.

- [ ] **Conflict archaeology (L).** A conflict opens with two small timelines, "this side added caching" and "that side changed ownership". Pick a point to see the smallest pair of commits that first made the branches conflict, found by pairwise test merges as git-imerge does.
  _Closest:_ [git-imerge](https://github.com/mhagger/git-imerge), a CLI.

- [ ] **Conflicts that can wait (L).** Run a rebase or restack in its own worktree, and show its conflicts on the graph's nodes. You can go do other work and come back. The original branches don't move until you accept the result.
  _Inspired by:_ [jj's first-class conflicts](https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/conflicts/), [VisualJJ](https://www.visualjj.com/).

- [ ] **Changelists (L).** Group what you're working on into named lists such as _Feature_, _Cleanup_ and _Debug prints_, each with its own draft message. Commit or set aside (shelve) one list and keep the others. Lists by file could come first; by hunk is harder once the files keep changing.
  _Seen in:_ [JetBrains changelists and shelve](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/idea/commit-and-push-changes.html).

- [ ] **Parallel branches in one folder (XL).** Work on several branches in the same checkout and give each hunk to a branch, as GitButler does. This is a different way of working, not a feature, so it should wait until the pieces above exist.
  _Seen in:_ [GitButler parallel branches](https://docs.gitbutler.com/features/branch-management/virtual-branches).
title: Ideas: reshaping history and stacked branches

body:
Ideas that make the scary parts of git safe to try: see what an operation will do before doing it, and get back what was lost after. They are only suggestions, so take whatever fits and close the rest.

I checked them against the README, the manual and `src/` on `dev`, and left out what gitcraft already has (undo / redo, confirmations, the conflict editor, Mergiraf). Effort is rough: **S** a contained addition, **M** a new view or a coordinated flow, **L** new state and recovery work.

## Most useful

- [ ] **"What will this do" before a destructive operation (S–M).** `repo/dialogs/confirm.rs` shows a title, a sentence and a red button. A hard reset says it throws away "the commits after this one", but not which ones or which files. The dialog would list:
  - the commits leaving the branch, each marked _still on branch x_ or _only here_;
  - the uncommitted files that will be lost;
  - _already pushed, a force push will be needed_ where it applies, rebases included;
  - the git commands it runs, folded;
  - _Ctrl+Z restores this_ when undo covers it.

- [ ] **Conflict warning before acting (S–M).** Commit and branch menus mark merge, rebase and cherry-pick as _conflicts in 3 files_ before you click. A toolbar badge shows when the current branch conflicts with its target. `git merge-tree --write-tree` (git 2.38+) answers this without touching the working tree, so it can run in the background, on WSL and SSH machines too. A hover says whether Mergiraf can solve it.
  _Seen in:_ [GitKraken Conflict Prevention](https://help.gitkraken.com/gitkraken-desktop/conflict-prevention), [Fork 2.56 / 2.66](https://fork.dev/releasenotes), [SmartGit 26.1 Commit Overlap](https://www.smartgit.dev/whats-new/26_1/).

- [ ] **Force push with lease when a push is refused, and Sync (S).** Quick edits, interactive rebase, amend and undo all rewrite history, but the toolbar's Push only runs a plain `git push`. Then it fails with "failed to push some refs" and the way out is the terminal. On a rejected push, show a banner such as _origin/dev has 3 commits you don't have_, with _Pull, then push_, _Force push (with lease)…_ and _Cancel_. A Sync button pulls, then pushes.
  _Seen in:_ [Tower](https://www.git-tower.com/features/all-features), [GitKraken](https://help.gitkraken.com/working-with/pushing-and-pulling/).

- [ ] **Reflog browser and lost-commit recovery (S–M).** A view of HEAD's and each branch's reflog, with times and what moved them. Select an entry to see its commit, then _Create branch here_ or cherry-pick it. Creating a branch is the default; resetting is not. A second scan finds dangling commits when the reflog is gone. This reaches what gitcraft's own undo can't: mistakes made in the terminal, in another client or in an earlier session.
  _Seen in:_ [Fork](https://fork.dev/releasenoteswin) (reflog entries in the graph), [Git Extensions](https://git-extensions-documentation.readthedocs.io/en/main/maintenance.html), Tower.

## Bigger

- [ ] **Ghost run: the result drawn on the graph (M–L).** Hover or hold Alt over Rebase, Reset hard, Pull, Force push, Delete branch or Drop commit. The graph draws the result as translucent "ghost" lanes over the real ones. A strip lists the commits that become unreachable (with their authors), the working-tree files that change, and which steps conflict. Let go and nothing has happened. Rebase and cherry-pick run in memory with `git replay` (git 2.44+) and a merge with `merge-tree`; older git falls back to a scratch worktree. `git rev-list old --not new` gives what is lost. The same engine would serve the rebase weather, collision radar and undo tree ideas below.
  _Closest:_ [GitSim](https://github.com/egekaya1/GitSimulator) (a CLI/TUI) and Mercurial's `rebase --dry-run`. No GUI does this in its own graph.

- [ ] **Rehearse an operation, tests included (M–L).** _Rehearse_ plays a rebase or merge through in a scratch clone and reports something like _stops at commit 7, two conflicts, `cargo test` fails_. Try a merge instead, compare the two outcomes, then pick one. Applying it checks that the refs haven't moved meanwhile and goes into the undo journal. This is the ghost run, but executed.

- [ ] **Rebase weather (M).** In the interactive-rebase list, each row gets a sun, a cloud or a storm for whether it applies cleanly at that position. The icons update while you move a commit, so you see the storm before you drop it. Hovering a storm names the conflicting files and says whether Mergiraf solves them. The todo list is replayed in memory, debounced, with results cached by (parent tree, commit).
  _Closest:_ [I-Rebase](https://github.com/13hakta/i-rebase), a VS Code extension with a manual "check conflicts" button based on file overlap.

- [ ] **Push preflight with identity guard (S–M).** Before a push, a short checklist catches:
  - a work email going to a personal remote (from the profile's author per host);
  - unsigned commits when the profile signs;
  - leftover `fixup!` or WIP commits;
  - likely secrets;
  - blobs over a few MB that belong in LFS;
  - _force push drops 2 commits by someone else_.

  Each item has a fix button (amend the author, autosquash, move to LFS), and Ctrl+Z undoes it.
  _Closest:_ hook-based checks such as [Git::MoreHooks](https://metacpan.org/pod/Git::MoreHooks::CheckCommitAuthorFromMailmap). None is in a GUI, and none knows about profiles.

- [ ] **Persistent operation timeline (M).** Undo lives in memory today, capped at 50 entries. Keep a timeline of gitcraft's operations, each with the refs before and after and the files it changed, across restarts: open yesterday's rebase and get the old branch tip back. Ref moves made elsewhere show up as observed events.
  _Seen in:_ [jj's operation log](https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/operation-log/), [GitButler Timeline](https://docs.gitbutler.com/features/timeline).

- [ ] **Undo tree (M).** Ctrl+Shift+Z shows the undo history as a branching tree, like Vim's undotree. Undo three steps and then do something new, and the old future becomes a branch instead of being lost. Hovering a node previews that state with the ghost-run renderer. The snapshots stay under `refs/gitcraft/undo/*` so gc doesn't prune them.

- [ ] **Undo one thing and keep the rest (L).** In the timeline, select yesterday's merge and choose _Remove this, keep later work_. gitcraft replays the later commits without it, in a scratch repository, and offers the result as a new branch with any conflicts shown. Start with local operations that only make commits.
  _Closest:_ selective undo in editors ([Azurite](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~NatProg/papers/ICSE15-Azurite-final.pdf)).

- [ ] **Rewrite receipt (M).** After a reorder, squash or rebase, a receipt says _final files identical, authors kept, two messages changed, signatures replaced_. Expand it to follow each old commit to its replacement. It compares tree IDs, maps the patches as `range-diff` does, and is kept with the undo entry.

- [ ] **Lost and found by content (S–M).** "I had a function `parse_header` on Tuesday and it's gone": type what you remember. gitcraft searches the reflogs, dropped stashes, dangling commits and dangling blobs (things once staged but never committed), and shows the hits on a timeline. Each one can come back as a branch, a file or a stash. It uses `git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs`, then `cat-file --batch` and a grep.
  _Closest:_ Git Extensions' _Recover lost objects_, which covers commits only.

- [ ] **Drafts of the working tree (L, opt-in).** Snapshot the working changes at pauses and before checkouts or rebases, without visible WIP commits. _Uncommitted changes_ gains _Earlier versions_, so a hunk overwritten by mistake can come back. The index stays separate, the snapshots are protected from gc, and old ones are cleared after a while.
  _Seen in:_ [jj's working-copy commit](https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/working-copy/), JetBrains' Local History.

- [ ] **Progress, cancel and an activity log (M).** Long operations show "Fetch…" and a spinner: no percentage, no cancel, and the whole toolbar is disabled while they run. Errors are cut to one line and only shown in full on hover. Instead:
  - run network operations with `--progress` and draw "Receiving objects: 45%" as a thin bar under the toolbar;
  - add _Cancel_, using the code that already stops a command that hangs;
  - add an **Activity** panel with each operation's command, how long it took and its full output, which can be copied.
title: Ideas: safety nets for scary operations (previews, conflict warnings, recovery)
